why: The gate must not block the agent from reading its own state; this is the exemption that was dead code in the previous implementation.

Regression guard for the return path of the new soft rule: after a turn that only asked a question the agent must be able to hand the machine back to ready. advance-to-executing allows every target in the agent list, and a command that only runs the entry script is control-plane, so this is already allowed today. The case pins that it stays allowed; it does not test the new prose, which nothing can execute.

The protected-list rule says nothing may MODIFY those paths. Judging every path a command mentions instead meant reading a human's file was refused, and after self-protection becomes unconditional it would also mean `python .github/ocf/ocf.py status` - which names the entry script on every call - could not run, leaving a gate nobody can read. This pins the distinction: the same path, read versus written.
Regression for the bypass where any command merely containing the entry name inherited the control-plane exemption.
Every statement must be the entry invocation, so appending real work to a control-plane command does not smuggle it through.
Regression for a command hidden at tool_input.task.command being invisible to the guard, which made create_and_run_task fail open.
The same command must still be caught in executing, where the approval rule no longer applies.

The self-authorization rule asks whether a human-only subcommand is being written into an executable file. Its pattern once allowed arbitrary text between the entry script's name and the verb, so a file that merely mentioned the entry script near an unrelated word beginning with `allow` was refused as self-authorization. The two words must be adjacent now.
Regression for the content scan that only read content/newString, so a human-only subcommand nested in replacements[].newString went unseen.
Regression for counting semicolons inside a hashtable literal, which produced false positives that blocked legitimate commands.
Parentheses are not a hiding place: the count must stay honest so the limit means something.
An unbalanced bracket must not blank the remainder of the command and hide what follows.
A control-plane command must not be able to authorize anything; order in the policy matters.

reload rewrites the instructions the model reads, so an agent able to run it could edit its own rules. It is derived from the human side of the command table rather than from a second list here, so this case also pins that the new command landed on the human side.

The rule reads the subcommand - the argument after the entry script - not the words anywhere in the text. Matching text anywhere denied an ordinary cleanup because a FILE happened to be named like a subcommand, which is the same defect class as judging an allow rule off a path that merely appears in a command.
Same fix, the other way round: the word is a search pattern, the entry script is never invoked. A rule keyed on the words alone would deny reading for the word protect.
The positive half of the same fix: the subcommand is still caught when it is not the first statement, so narrowing the match to the argument position did not narrow it into an escape hatch.
The machine never looks at an image with a tool, not even while acting.
A newly added tool that carries a command must be judged as an exec tool, or it runs uninspected.
Reading must stay possible while asking, otherwise intake cannot be done at all.
The baseline promise: nothing runs before the human approves.
The same promise for edits.
The gate itself demands plan.md, so it must be writable while the plan is still being written.

The protected list is tied to the switch, not to approval, so it must still hold during executing. The list carries the orchestrator's own files now, and `touches-protected` is what refuses - the same rule that refuses every other protected path, which is the whole point of having one list.

Every rule follows the master switch, the protected list included, so with the window open gate code is editable - which is what the window is for. What keeps that safe is that only a human can open it, not that the list ignores the switch. With the switch ON the same write is refused, and self-protection-holds-while-acting is what pins that half. The master switch now answers with SILENCE rather than `allow`, and that half matters as much as the edit does: `allow` is a hook suppressing the editor's own approval prompt, which is more permissive than having no gate at all, so a disarmed gate must say nothing at all. The edit still goes through, because nothing refuses it, which is what this case has always been about.
A glob entry in the protected list must protect the whole subtree.

The exemption mechanism is gone by design: allowed_edits is still set here and it must NOT lift the block. A list that can be pointed away is not a list, and this pins that the second file no longer has any power.
Terminal discipline: everything stays visible to the human.
Long commands are where output ownership and quoting go wrong.
The same command for the fourth time suggests a loop; the human decides, so this answers ask.
An unreadable policy must fail towards denying, never towards an open gate.
These four tools shape the conversation and cannot touch the repository, which is what the session class means; the gate must not ask the human about them.

Regression: a listed_in precondition judged over the whole batch let one protected path drag every other path into the denial. The batch here touches no protected path at all, while the list does name one.

T9: the file carrying the standing contract was on the protected list and simultaneously exempted in the old allowed-edits file, so the net effect was permission for the machine to rewrite it. It is on the protected list now, and there is no exemption mechanism left anywhere to lift that. The legacy exemption fields are left in place on purpose: this case proves they no longer have any power.
When a batch really does touch a protected path, the block must name that file rather than some other file in the same batch.

Regression: this command and the readable one below are the same write. Both reached the path rules as an empty candidate list, so this one - the easier spelling to reach for - was allowed while the other was refused. Writing is now known from the command text, and a write whose target could not be read is refused instead of passing as touching nothing.

The third answer must not swallow the readable case. This is the same write with the target written out, so the protected-list rule names the file rather than the generic rule saying the target could not be read.
The boundary on the other side: a command with no write verb in it answers `none`, not `unknown`, so the new rule stays out of the way and the environment rules decide.

The redirect test read the raw command string, so any `>` counted - including one inside a closed pair of quotes, where no shell treats it as a redirect. `git commit -m "a->b"` was therefore a write whose target could not be read: refused, with advice that cannot be followed, since that command has no path to name. Only a redirect outside quotes is a redirect now.

The other side of the same fix. Stripping quoted spans is only safe while the quotes balance; an unterminated quote is precisely the case where `>` may still redirect, so the command is read as written and the write is judged as before.

A shell left at a continuation prompt is the exact shape of a command that hung with no echo. The gate reads text and cannot predict that an unclosed quote will hang a shell, so it notices the aftermath instead.
A command moved to the background has not reported a result, so treating it as a completed success is a silent error.

payload.tool_response: Note: This terminal execution was moved to the background using the ID 1234.

why: The exit code is the one machine fact the editor hands back about how a command went, and it arrives in the tool response as text. Counting it means a failure is recorded even when the model does not notice one - the case the budget was blind to, because only the model's own `fail` call ever moved the counter before.
The other side of the count. A command that exited 0 is not added to the budget, so an ordinary successful run cannot arm it.

`grep` returns 1 for 'no match' and `diff` for 'they differ'. That 1 is the answer to the question the command was asked, not a failure, so the first word decides whether the exit code is a verdict at all.
A command that reported normally must not be warned about, or the injection becomes noise the human learns to ignore.

payload.tool_response:
On branch master
nothing to commit, working tree clean

why: Only commands can hang; a file edit has no output to wait for.

Regression for a live lockout: a one-character policy typo made the strict fallback deny read_file as well, so the agent could neither see the file nor help repair it. Denying every change is the point; denying reading protects nothing and blinds everyone.
The strict fallback must keep the session and read tools, or a broken policy removes any way to record, ask about or reason about the problem.

`zero-p0` is the gate that lets work start, so whoever can write the number can open the gate. The agent that wrote the plan is the party the audit checks, so it is the last one that may write this particular fact. The hook reads the count off the auditor's report instead.
The rule above has to be about this one fact and not about `set`. A rule that quietly banned every fact would look the same on the case that blocks the number, and the intake is built out of facts.

The budget is what turns repeated failure into a stop. Only the hook arms this fact, and until this case nothing drove the armed state, so the rule was free to stop matching without anything going red.
Entering executing is the human's act, and it is the one state the agent can never reach. The rule reads the command text, so this pins the spelling that actually comes out of an agent's terminal.

tool_input.command: python .github/ocf/ocf.py advance executing "the plan looks fine to me"

why: A command that blocks on input, or raises an elevation prompt, hangs the turn with nothing to show for it. The gate cannot see the prompt coming, so it judges the spellings that produce one.

Running the suite is how an agent grades its own work, and the rule is that the human asks first. No fixture ever sets the fact, so this case pins the refusing half - which is the whole point of the rule.

The gate must not let the machine pick a toolchain on the human's behalf. `undeclared-env-tool` covers the tools that exist to do this; this is its terminal counterpart, and the two are judged by different classes, so neither case covers the other.
Every entry in that list is irreversible, and the rule is the only thing between an agent and one of them.

The same duty as the command rule above and a different class: this one is for the tools that exist only to change the toolchain. A class-keyed rule with no case is a rule nobody would notice had stopped matching.

The environment is declared here so the rule above it cannot fire, which is what makes this case about approval rather than about declaration. The three approval rules share one verdict and are keyed to three classes, so the only way to pin that this class reaches it is to walk one.

The host's key map accepts `PreToolUse` and `preToolUse` for one event, and the engine used to match the exact string - so a host that spelled it the other way got a hook that was installed, wired, and answered nothing. That failure is silent by construction: no decision looks exactly like no objection.

`reporting` is the one state in which the work is finished but the round is not: the contract's last step of a round is `advance ready`. Refusing the stop there is the narrowest enforcement that is still worth having, and it is also the shape check - Stop reads `decision`, not `permissionDecision`, so an engine that answered in the gate's shape would be ignored and the agent would stop as if nothing had objected.

The other half of the case above, and the half that keeps the rule from being a trap: in `executing` the agent stops to wait for the human, so refusing there would trap it in a loop it never earned. Silence is the answer.

The master switch has to control the whole system, and it did not: the entry point ran anyway, and a fault in it denied every call including the ones that would have recorded what happened. Off now means the gate is out of the way - and it says so, because with no decision and no statement of being disarmed, a gate a human switched off is indistinguishable from a gate that died.

PreCompact, SessionEnd and ErrorOccurred have no consumer on the other side, so anything written to stdout is parsed by nobody. They are recorded in the journal instead, and this case pins that they stay mute - an event that started answering would look healthy while doing nothing with the answer.

`[hooks] enabled = false` is what 'uninstall' means, and it must be honest rather than permissive: a hook answering `allow` would suppress the editor's own approval prompt, leaving the user with less protection than if they had never installed this at all. So the answer is silence.
